entries.claim: The bad loop count is caused by a use-after-free: the memory was released and handed to another object.
entries.evidence: The writers are sub_001F7930 iterating a list and updating each element via MEM32(esi + 8) - a field, not an object base. Nothing was freed. investigate.py's classifier asserted this and was wrong.

entries.claim: Skipping the dispatch loop is free, because every call in it targets 0 and fails, so the loop achieves nothing.
entries.evidence: Measured 1452 -> 56 kernel calls against an unchanged seed list. 'Every call fails' is not 'the loop has no effect' - it still advances an index and the failing calls run through the safe stub, which touches esp and eax.

entries.claim: The 16-byte allocation is failing and returning null.
entries.evidence: The allocation site is a clean operator-new plus constructor and it succeeds; 0x030FEFE8 is a legitimately allocated buffer.

entries.claim: esp escaping the 8 MB stack means the stack is corrupted.
entries.evidence: 0x03DAB1C8 is the worker thread's own stack, allocated from guest heap by PsCreateSystemThreadEx. triage_crash's heuristic does not model the second thread.

entries.claim: Engine global 0x5BC508 is never initialised.
entries.evidence: Written once by sub_00239E50+0x15C, before the loop that reads it.

entries.claim: The boot is deterministic, so a single run is a sound measurement.
entries.evidence: The three gated counters repeat exactly, but total dispatch volume swings 8x between runs (622M vs 74.9M). Stable where the gate looks; not stable in general.

entries.claim: kernel_calls is an adequate progress signal.
entries.evidence: It read exactly 1452 across 566 seeded functions, 31 lifter repairs and a fixed freeze. It saturates where the boot stops. Replaced as the primary gate by `reached` (distinct dispatch targets), first measurement 692.

entries.claim: A missing function is what blocks the boot.
entries.evidence: 566 functions that vtables provably call were seeded and measured safe; kernel_calls did not move. Worth re-testing against `reached`, which did not exist at the time.

entries.claim: The loop's count field is an end-pointer of a begin/end range over an array of function pointers
entries.evidence: Measured the memory the pointers bracket: MEM32(0x00F81180)=0x00F84600 (back-pointer to the object), +4=0x00F812B0, +8=0x00F81188 (self-pointer). Heap pointers, not code addresses. Not a function-pointer array.

entries.claim: registry+0x2C is maintained as a linked-list head by sub_0019FBC7 but read as an {array,count} descriptor by the loop in sub_001F7930
entries.evidence: Object at 0x00F84600 = {0x00F812B0, 0x00F81180, 0, 0}; the memory it points to contains a self-pointer (0x00F81188 -> itself) and a back-pointer to the object - the classic empty-list sentinel shape. sub_0019FBC7 does list splicing (MEM32(ecx)=esi; MEM32(edx)=ecx; MEM32(esi+4)=ecx) and is the writer of that pointer. BOTH functions are faithfully lifted per faithful.py, so neither side is a translation bug. Open fork: whether sub_0019FBC7 legitimately owns that field, or has a wrong pointer.

entries.claim: registry+0x28 and +0x2C are one embedded list head, so the loop reads half of a two-word structure
entries.evidence: Dumped registry+0x24..+0x30 at loop entry: +0x24=0, +0x28=0, +0x2C=0x00F84600, +0x30=0x00F81288. +0x28 is zero, so it is not the other half of a list head. Note +0x30 holds the registry's OWN base address - a self-reference not yet explained.

entries.claim: sub_0019FBC7 is game code maintaining a linked list, and registry+0x2C is either its list head or its victim
entries.evidence: Call stack proves sub_0019FBC7 is the HEAP ALLOCATOR's internal list manager: sub_0019FBC7 <- sub_001A0B0C <- sub_003437C7 <- sub_003437F3 (operator new) <- sub_00216251 <- sub_00236500 <- sub_00239E50. It is free-list bookkeeping, not game logic.

entries.claim: The heap allocator writes its own free-list links INSIDE the registry's live memory block
entries.evidence: Probe at the splice site fired with eax=0x00F81358, node=0x00F81360, registry base (MEM32(0x5BC508))=0x00F81288, offset=0xD0. So a node was spliced at registry+0xD8 while the registry pointer was already set. Either the registry block was freed and returned to the free list, or the allocator's bookkeeping is writing out of bounds. Not yet distinguished - do not act on this until it is.

entries.claim: The engine allocator (sub_003437F3) returns the SAME address for multiple distinct allocations
entries.evidence: Direct measurement with a duplicate detector on every return: 7 allocations, 4 distinct, 3 duplicates. 0x00F81288 was returned on allocations #3, #4 and #6 as well as its first. So several live objects occupy one block and overwrite each other. This is the root cause of the registry's fields holding heap pointers, the free-list links found inside it, and the bogus 16-million count - all of them are other objects' data in the same memory.

entries.claim: Probes and logging calls inserted into generated code are behaviourally free
entries.evidence: Adding recomp_alloc_log/recomp_alloc_fixup calls at the allocator's return in sub_003437F3 made the boot die at 33 kernel calls in 2 of 3 runs. Removing them: 5 of 5 runs at 692/1452/152/11, exactly stable. Causation established by removal. The allocator return is not a safe place to call out to C - likely stdio locking or timing, since stdio locks have deadlocked this boot before.

entries.claim: The 7-allocations/3-duplicates measurement describes the clean boot
entries.evidence: That measurement was taken WITH the allocator instrumentation in place, and the instrumentation is now proven to perturb the boot (2 of 3 runs died early). The duplicate returns are a direct observation so they are probably real, but the count and ordering were recorded on a disturbed system and must be re-measured without perturbing the allocator before anything is built on them.

entries.claim: Setting the CRT __active_heap flag (0x6F12E0) to 1 gets the boot past the wall
entries.evidence: The flag really was 0 - four readers in generated code, zero writers - so this was a genuine missing initialisation and the fix is kept. But the boot is unchanged: 692/1452/152/11 on 3 of 3 runs. The heap mode was not what blocks the boot.

entries.claim: Ledger #16's allocator numbers reproduce exactly on an UNDISTURBED boot, resolving #18's doubt
entries.evidence:
Re-measured with a memory-only ring (two plain stores at sub_003437F3's return, no C call, so #17's failure mode cannot apply). Signals stayed 1452/152/11 deterministic across runs, identical to baseline - the instrumentation does not perturb. Result: 7 successful allocations, 4 distinct, 3 duplicates, all three being 0x00F81288 on the 3rd, 4th and 6th allocation. That is #16's measurement to the digit. #18 can be closed: the numbers were real, not an artefact.</evidence>

entries.claim: The engine allocator fails 690 of 697 times: after the 7th allocation every subsequent request returns NULL, and this is the dominant blocker
entries.evidence:
Full ring dump on an undisturbed boot (1452/152/11 deterministic): allocations 0-6 succeed (0x00F81730, 0x00F81288 x4, 0x00F81B28, 0x00F835C8), then allocations 7 through 696 ALL return 0x00000000 - 690 consecutive failures with no recovery. Ledger #16 never saw this because its instrumentation only counted successful returns. The last successful allocation, 0x00F835C8, is the pool head that progress.json records as having a 1.25MB limit with ZERO consumed - so the pool has capacity and refuses anyway, matching the explicit refusal already traced to sub_001EC9C0 returning 0xFFFFFFFF via sub_001F09D0 vtable+0x6C. NOTE the earlier duplicate-detector reported these NULLs as "63 duplicate returns" and concluded objects shared a block; repeated NULL is failure, not sharing, and the two are now counted separately.</evidence>
<parameter name="tags">allocator,sub_003437F3,allocation-failure,pool,sub_001F09D0

entries.claim: sub_001F7930 is correct code; the wall is that registry+0x2C holds a list-node pointer where the function expects a {function-table, count} descriptor
entries.evidence:
Ghidra decompilation of 0x001F7930 (created as wall_sub_001F7930, 281 bytes) reads: iVar1 = *(int *)(*(int *)(_DAT_005bc508 + 0x2c) + 4); then calls (**(code **)(*(int *)*puVar7 + iVar6 * 4))() while iVar6 < iVar1. So obj=MEM32(registry+0x2C), table=MEM32(obj), count=MEM32(obj+4), call table[i]. Ordinary descriptor iteration, and Ghidra's C matches the lifted C exactly, which is why faithful.py clears it. The same function's FIRST loop uses the same idea with array at +8 and count at +0xC on this+0x28, so descriptors of this shape are real in this engine. Measured count is 0x00F81180, a heap address, so 0 < count passes and the loop runs ~16.2M times. The defect is the DATA at registry+0x2C, not the code reading it.</evidence>
<parameter name="tags">sub_001F7930,ghidra,decompilation,registry,descriptor

entries.claim: The first write to registry+0x2C comes from a system DLL (a CRT memset/memcpy), not from lifted game code
entries.evidence:
run --watch 0x00F812B4:4:reg2C fired once: armed with current value 0x00000000, then "write to xbox VA 0x00F812B4 from RIP=0x7FFDFE5BE579 (RVA=0x67367E579)". That RVA is nonsense because the writer is outside our image, which is exactly how a system-DLL writer presents - matching investigation_report.md, which attributed several writes at 0x00F81288 to a CRT memset/memcpy. A bulk CRT write over the registry's fields is what constructing ANOTHER object at that base looks like, which fits #22 (0x00F81288 handed out 4 times). LIMITS, do not overstate: the watch disarms after one hit, so this is only the FIRST write, taken when the field still read 0 - it is not proven to be the write that installs the bad pointer, and the guest-side caller was not resolved. Next step to close it: recomp_where at the suspected constructor plus triage_crash.py --where, which is how the lock callers were named previously.</evidence>

entries.claim: The 690 allocation failures come from sub_001FE770 (vtable+0x6C) returning false on a zero size
entries.evidence:
Probed edx at sub_001FE770's size test (recomp_0015.c:5209). It fires EXACTLY ONCE per boot, with size=0x00140000 - 1.25MB, which is the pool size progress.json already records. So it takes the non-zero path and succeeds; the zero-size early-out never happens. More importantly the call count kills the wider story: vtable+0x6C is pool SETUP, called once, not the per-allocation path, so it cannot account for 690 failures. Signals unchanged at 1452/152/11 deterministic with the probe in place. NOTE for whoever picks this up: progress.json traced the chain sub_001F6FB0 -> ... -> sub_001F09D0 -> vtable+0x6C for ONE failure, and that trace is not evidence about the other 689. Where the bulk of the NULLs are produced is still unknown - counting them per return site is the honest next step, not following the single traced chain further.</evidence>

entries.claim: All 690 allocation failures come from sub_001A02B7 (the free-block finder) returning 0, counted not inferred
entries.evidence:
Counted with probes at every failure route inside sub_001A0B0C (lifted RtlAllocateHeap). Totals on one deterministic boot (1452/152/11): 690 NULL returns, matching the allocator ring exactly. Route A (heap-not-growable, MEM8(esi+0x14)&2 at recomp_0011.c:31527) fired 0 times. Route C (kernel call through MEM32(0x3C6CB8) returning negative, :31550) fired 0 times - the allocator NEVER reaches the kernel. Route B fired 690/690: recomp_0011.c:31523 sets STATUS_NO_MEMORY (0xC0000017) and returns NULL. Exactly one branch reaches route B - :31117 `if (eax == 0) goto loc_001A113A` - and eax there is the return of sub_001A02B7, called at :31113. Full chain, every link measured: sub_003437F3 (operator new) -> sub_003437C7 (retry loop) -> sub_003437A0 -> sub_001A0B0C -> sub_001A02B7 -> 0. DEBUGGING_NOTES.md:283 already names sub_001A02B7 as the heap's own block finder. NOTE two hypotheses died here: heap-not-growable and kernel-refusal, both 0 of 690.</evidence>
<parameter name="tags">sub_001A02B7,sub_001A0B0C,allocator,allocation-failure,RtlAllocateHeap

entries.claim: Replacing the CRT RtlAllocateHeap with the native heap fixes the allocation failures, the duplicate addresses and the sub_001F7930 spin together
entries.evidence:
sub_001A0B0C overridden in recomp_manual.c to call xbox_HeapAlloc (~55MB) instead of walking the guest free list; generated body stubbed by stub_overridden.py. Deterministic on 2 of 2 runs. kernel_calls 1452 -> 4000, failed_icalls 152 -> 2, heap_allocs 11 -> 13, safe_stub 192 -> 8, distinct kernel fns 15 -> 16. Allocator ring: 7 allocations, 0 failed, 0 duplicate - was 697/690/3. Indirect dispatches 677,120,348 -> 672, so the 600M-dispatch spin at sub_001F7930 is GONE, which confirms it was downstream of the allocator exactly as ledger #24 argued (correct code reading corrupted data). #22 (0x00F81288 returned four times) is settled by construction - a bump allocator cannot repeat an address. NEW WALL, further along: crash in sub_0020F209+0x176B writing 0xF687BE15. That is the engine's own pool carver, and it is the predicted consequence of handing out blocks with no NT block header - anything stepping back from a block to read one now finds unrelated memory. CAVEATS, both real: xbox_HeapAlloc only bumps, so RtlFreeHeap is now a leak (fine for reaching a menu with 55MB, not fine to ship); and only HEAP_ZERO_MEMORY is honoured of the flags.</evidence>
<parameter name="tags">sub_001A0B0C,allocator,override,recomp_manual,sub_001F7930,port-fix

entries.claim: Reporting real contiguous region extents from NtQueryVirtualMemory (instead of a flat 64KB) fixes the memory-walk hang
entries.evidence:
Replaced the flat 0x10000 RegionSize with the true extents from xbox_memory_layout.h - four regions (low memory, XBE image, 8MB stack, heap to end of RAM) plus a catch-all above 0x04000000 reporting free to the top of the address space. Reasoning was that a 64MB walk in 64KB steps needs ~1000 iterations and never finished, so real extents should take five. Measured, deterministic 2 of 2: kernel_calls COLLAPSED 4000 -> 58, safe_stub 1 -> 8, failed_icalls 1 -> 2, and the crash came back (access violation at RVA 0xD247F0). heap_allocs rose 13 -> 18, so it is doing something different early, not simply dying sooner. Reverted immediately per rule #14; the flat-64KB version restored 4000/1/13/1 with no crash on 2 of 2, so the regression is entirely attributable to this change. NOT YET DIAGNOSED - candidates worth separating before retrying: (a) the ~49MB heap reported as ONE committed region may make the caller believe a huge contiguous block exists and act on it, (b) the above-RAM catch-all computes size as 0xFFFFFFFF - base which is close to overflow and may wrap in the caller's arithmetic, (c) reporting region_base BELOW the queried address (true extents start low, the granule version did not) may break a walker that assumes BaseAddress <= returned base. Do not simply re-apply this whole change; test (b) alone first, it is the cheapest and the most likely to be an outright bug in my code rather than a semantic mismatch.</evidence>
<parameter name="tags">NtQueryVirtualMemory,ordinal-217,kernel-bridge,region-size,regression

entries.claim: The ~1000x repeated memory scan is driven by sub_001F09D0's retry loop, whose exit condition tests the global 0x5BC5D8
entries.evidence:
Named with recomp_where from inside bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory, then resolved by triage_crash.py --where. A sampled watchdog RIP could not do this - it only ever landed in kernel_thunk_dispatch, because 3,968 of 4,000 calls funnel through our own bridge. Full chain, identical on every captured call: bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory <- kernel_thunk_dispatch <- sub_0034D457 <- sub_001FFDA1 <- sub_001F09D0 <- sub_001EC9D8 <- sub_0020F209 <- sub_0020EFD0 <- sub_0020F860 <- sub_00211530 <- sub_001EC5E0 <- sub_001EC120 <- sub_0021644B <- sub_00216251 <- sub_00236500 <- sub_00239E50 <- sub_00011E40, under bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx. sub_001F09D0 is the SAME function decompiled earlier this session (ledger #27 context): a do/while retry loop whose failure exits all return 0xFFFFFFFF, and whose continue/exit condition compares a value against _DAT_005bc5d8. That global was examined separately earlier today and is BSS with exactly ONE writer in the whole tree - recomp_0017.c:2652, inside sub_00239E50, which stores ZERO - against ~250 read sites. So the loop is very likely testing against a sentinel that never gets its real value. NOT YET PROVEN: that the zero is wrong rather than a legitimate null sentinel. The cheap decisive test is to probe the compared value and _DAT_005bc5d8 at the loop head in sub_001F09D0 and see whether they can ever match.</evidence>
<parameter name="tags">sub_001F09D0,0x5BC5D8,NtQueryVirtualMemory,retry-loop,hang

entries.claim: CORRECTION to #31: sub_001F09D0's loop-back at loc_001F0AC7 and the 0x5BC5D8 sentinel are NOT what spins
entries.evidence:
Probed loc_001F0AC7 in recomp_0014.c printing eax, MEM32(eax) and MEM32(0x5BC5D8), limit 8. It fired ZERO times on a full run (4000/1/13/1, deterministic), so that branch is never reached and the 0x5BC5D8 comparison cannot be driving the repetition. #31's backtrace is still correct and stands - sub_001F09D0 IS on the chain under the repeated NtQueryVirtualMemory calls - but it is CALLED BY the loop, not the loop itself. The retry cycle sits above it and was already documented on 2026-08-05: sub_0020F0B2 is the retry-loop head, and sub_0020F209's three early exits are all "memory was reclaimed, go round again", making the engine allocator a CYCLE rather than a chain. So the shape is: sub_0020EFD0 -> sub_0020F209 -> (growth attempt: sub_001EC9D8 -> sub_001F09D0 -> NtQueryVirtualMemory) -> growth fails -> sub_0020F0B2 -> round again. The open question is why the engine's pool growth cannot be satisfied, one layer above the CRT heap that #29 fixed.</evidence>
<parameter name="tags">sub_001F09D0,0x5BC5D8,sub_0020F0B2,sub_0020F209,correction,retry-loop
